newsitem.title: CHINA: China copper plant closure to impact raw materials.
newsitem.headline: China copper plant closure to impact raw materials.

text.p: China's imports of copper raw materials could be affected by the closure of a local, private copper producer, though the effect on the refined metal market would be negligible, traders said on Wednesday.
China's imports of blister and scrap, both raw materials in the production of refined copper, have been drastically reduced this year in a sluggish market atmosphere.
The exit of a buyer of up to 30,000 tonnes of blister and another 30,000 tonnes (copper content) of scrap would make a decent dent in the world market, industry sources said.
Taicang Copper Co in eastern Jiangsu province closed in January over a tax dispute involving tolling licences, sources in Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore and London said.
Tolling is the import of raw materials for processing and re-exporting. Raw materials for tolling can be imported to China free of duty and value-added tax.
Customs authorities in picturesque Suzhou, in Jiangsu, said Taicang had been importing raw materials on tolling licences but selling the finished product on the domestic market.
A customs official declined to say how much import duty was payable on the imports, or to give any further details.

One of the London-based sources said Taicang was being investigated for avoiding more than 50 million yuan ($6 million) in import and value-added taxes. These charges add 21 percent to the cost of imported copper.
"The impact (of Taicang's closure) won't be felt too much in the refined metal market, but it will be much greater in the raw materials market, particularly blister," an analyst in London said.

"China has taken hardly any blister so far this year. One of the reasons for this is Taicang -- they usually take around 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes (a year) and with them being removed from the market, that will leave a big hole," he said.
A source in Hong Kong with a Chinese government trading company said Taicang imported up to 30,000 tonnes of blister a year.

An analyst with Macquarie Equities said earlier this year that China's copper supplies totalled 1.417 million tonnes in 1996, up nine percent on 1995, with 967,000 tonnes coming from imports of scrap, blister and cathode.
A source at Macquarie Bank in London said scrap accounted for 211,000 tonnes and blister for 113,000 tonnes of China's 1996 imports.
"So 30,000 tonnes out of either of those figures is quite a significant figure," he said, adding that the copper content of China's scrap imports was arguably between 30 and 50 percent.
Customs figures show imports of uncast and raw copper rose 28.2 percent to 77,885 tonnes in the first two months of 1997.
Total 1996 imports of uncast copper and copper products, according to customs figures, were 714,248 tonnes, up 32.7 percent on 1995.
No one from Taicang, which is said to have a purchasing office in the United States, could be reached. The telephone number for the factory remains unanswered.
After the factory's closure, assets were seized and auctioned, the sources said. Around 32 million yuan was still owed, one source said.
It produced 70,000 to 80,000 tonnes of refined copper in 1996, for supply to the Shanghai market, the London analyst said.
The impact on the metal market of Taicang's closure has not been great because both demand and cash were low, Chinese analysts in Shanghai said.
The local metal market had been sluggish since early 1997 and did not look like picking up before the second half, a researcher with a Shanghai firm said.

Most smelters were covered until mid-1997, and one of the biggest, Jinlong -- in which Japan's Sumitomo and Itochu Corp have interests and due to begin production in May -- was covered to the end of the year, a supplier source said.
($1=8.3 Chinese yuan)
